newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore hotels seen hit by slow visitor growth.
newsitem.headline: Singapore hotels seen hit by slow visitor growth.

text.p: Singapore hotels are likely to feel increasingly squeezed between the slowdown in visitor arrivals to the city-state and the burgeoning supply of hotel rooms, industry analysts and officials say.

The strength of the Singapore dollar, slower economic growth in some Asian countries and increased regional competition for the tourist dollar have all contributed to a downturn in visitor arrivals in recent months, they said.

"We've probably lost about three to five percent of our business over the last three months," said Michael Tan, director of marketing at the Mandarin Hotel, adding that room occupancy had slipped to around 80 percent as a result.
Tourist arrivals in Singapore fell for the third straight month in September, according to the latest data from the Singapore Tourist Promotion Board (STPB).

Total visitor arrivals for the first nine months of 1996 were up 1.5 percent to 5.4 million from a year ago, but show few signs of returning to the more than seven percent annual growth rates of 1993 and 1994 after falling to 3.4 percent last year.

An STPB spokeswoman said the tourism board expected to meet its projected growth rate of three to five percent in visitor arrivals this year, with preliminary data for October showing an increase of just over two percent.
But analysts said hotels would come under increased pressure to cut room rates to sustain occupancy levels in the face of a downturn in visitor arrivals and intensifying competition.

Pearly Yap, a hotel industry analyst at Crosby Securities, said average room rates were likely to fall by two percent this year and by four to five percent in 1997 and 1998, with the larger, deluxe hotels seen as the most vulnerable.
She said new hotels were likely to offer packages at a 40 percent discount from their listed prices for three- to six-month periods, resulting in price pressure on older hotels.
Growth in the supply of hotel rooms will average 9.1 percent over the next three years until 1998, compared with average growth of 3.6 percent between 1993 and 1995, Yap said.

She said the decline in Asian arrivals, the largest segment of Singapore's tourist market, was due partly to the growing popularity of Hong Kong ahead of its 1997 handover to China and Malaysia's aggressive promotion of its own tourism industry.
"The perception is that we're really not a city for leisure," said Janet Tan-Collis, a vice president with the National Association of Travel Agents.
She said Singapore was increasingly losing out to competing tourist destinations, partly because it lacked the sizzle of cities like New York, London and Hong Kong.
"All the hoteliers have been very conservative in their rate increases for 1997," she added.

Michael Tan said the Mandarin Hotel had not lowered its room rates so far, and was dealing with the business slowdown through cost-cutting measures, including not replacing personnel lost through attrition.
A spokesman for The Westin Stamford and Westin Plaza hotels said they were holding room rates steady and had not experienced a slowdown in occupancy.
"Obviously, the easiest thing is to down the room rates, but I think there's a floor to that because of cost levels," said an analyst with a local broking house.
He said hotels should step up marketing efforts by drawing on their international networks instead.
The STPB's ambitious "Tourism 21" plan, which aims to attract 10 million visitors annually by 2000, was also likely to bring relief to hoteliers in the longer term, he said.
